doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

chapter: Career and the business of an unusual instrument
title: Unusual instrument as gift and curse, booking difficulties
summary: Rowe compares Scales with Howard Levy and Bela Fleck; Scales says the pan draws curiosity but promoters pass on what they do not understand, and NPR Tiny Desk came from a producer seeing them live.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: I do. And it’s interesting because I’ve been able to speak with Howard Levy and Bela Fleck and the three of you are playing an instrument that you’ve stretched the boundaries of, and not necessarily the everyday oh saxophone, piano, trumpet. Do you believe that that distinction is a plus in some ways and a minus in others as far as marketing?

Oh yes. Yes. It’s a gift and a curse. Because the gift is, “Oh wow, like how is this person doing this on this instrument that I’ve never seen before. I’m instantly drawn into this. Like this looks cool, what could this possibly be?” So you do get that side of it, right? But

then the curse side is there are people who they don’t really know what we do because they’ve never seen it. So there’s festival promoters and organizers who, they’re like yeah we’re going to pass on this Jonathan Scales thing because they don’t know what it is. They don’t understand. You see what I’m saying? So like in some ways – so I’m able to have a sustainable career because we – there’s enough people who like they understand what we do enough to allow us to have opportunities. However, there’s still a lot of like doors that are just slammed in our face that we can’t get to the other side of because they just don’t grasp the concepts of what we’re doing. Because it’s not easily compared to something else. You can’t be like, “Oh yeah, it’s kind of like this band.” And also they don’t know about the steel pan so like there are some people who like, “Yeah the steel pan is a cool instrument but like I don't know if I want that at my event, not knowing that like I’m playing it as an instrument. Like it’s not about the instrument it’s about the self- expression of what we’re trying to play as a unit and as a composer and as musicians. Right? So the instrument does get pigeonholed sometimes where there’s opportunities that don’t come about because someone doesn’t even give it the time of day. You see what I’m saying?
I do. Yes I understand that. And have you had people who’ve considered booking you but say, “Listen I like it but can’t you bring a fourth player like I heard on one of your records?”

I will say at this point that’s not really a conversation that comes up just because like I think that like at this point anyone who gets that far in the conversation of like trying to book us knows what they’re getting into.

And then before that either someone knows what they’re getting into or they don’t know what they’re getting into. And if they don’t know what they’re getting into sometimes they won’t even – we’re not in the conversation at all. So it’s been a slow process over time. So I would say it’s less of a thing where people are like, “Well if you did this then maybe we can –” you know. And it’s more along the lines of like people don’t – it’s like seeing is believing or something you know. So sometimes people have to see it before they can like connect to it and like understand. For example like we did the NPR Tiny Desk thing. And I got – we got on NPR’s Tiny Desk because one of the producers saw us in real life. One of the producers of Tiny Desk happened to be in the room where we performed somewhere and they were in the crowd and they saw us. It’s not because we submitted an application. You see what I’m saying? Because my band on an application looks like, “What is this? It doesn’t make sense.” So any success that we’ve come across is because someone saw us and was curious and wants to know more and then brought us in. You know?
